lead: Bending loss is the extra attenuation caused when an optical fiber is curved. The guided light no longer sees a perfectly straight core, so part of its field reaches the cladding and escapes. Two forms exist: macro bending, where the whole fiber follows a large curve, and micro bending, where small random wiggles disturb the core. Every installed cable has bends at trays, cabinets and wall corners. Bending loss tells the designer how tight a bend is safe before the received power falls below the receiver's sensitivity.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for dB and loss budgets, and Unit 1 for total internal reflection, critical angle and numerical aperture.

blocks.text: Macro bending, also called macrocurvature loss, happens when the whole fiber follows a curve of radius R. On the outside of the curve, the guided mode must bend around the corner. Its phase front tilts and its tail extends further into the cladding. If that tail is beyond the region where total internal reflection can hold it, light tunnels out and radiates away. The loss grows as R falls.

blocks.where: α_bend is the bend loss per turn in dB; R is the bend radius in mm; A is a constant in dB per turn for that fiber and wavelength; B is a constant in mm⁻¹. A and B come from measurement, not from a universal table.

blocks.text: The curve is flat at large R and turns upward sharply near a critical radius R_c. A useful estimate is:

blocks.where: R_c is the critical bend radius; n₁ is the core refractive index; n₂ is the cladding refractive index; λ is the free-space wavelength in the same length unit as R_c; π is the constant 3.1416.

blocks.text: Below R_c, loss per turn becomes large; above it, loss is usually small. A common shop-floor check wraps a few turns around a 10 mm mandrel and measures the added loss. A 10 mm radius may be harmless; a 5 mm radius can already cost noticeable loss at 1550 nm. Cable trays, splice cassettes, wall corners and spare-fiber loops are the usual places where R becomes too small.

Micro bending, or microcurvature loss, comes from many small random bends along the fiber. The coating, cabling, temperature changes and lateral pressure can all create them. Each wiggle is tiny, but together they act like a weak grating. They couple the guided core mode to cladding modes and radiation modes, so power leaks out along the length.

Macro bending

blocks.text: Bending loss rises with wavelength. At 1550 nm the mode field is wider and reaches further into the cladding than at 1310 nm, so a 1550 nm system suffers more from the same bend. This is one reason 1310 nm links tolerate tighter installation than 1550 nm links.

Bend-insensitive fiber adds a low-index trench in the cladding. The trench pulls the mode back toward the core, so less field reaches the outer cladding at a bend. Such fiber is used in drop cables, patch cords and crowded data-center trays.

The standard test is still simple: wrap a few turns around a mandrel, measure power with and without the wrap, and divide by the number of turns. Record the wavelength, radius and number of turns with the result.

sections.h3: Using bend loss in a link budget

blocks.text: Bend loss is quoted as dB per turn at a stated radius and wavelength. It is not a loss per kilometre. Before adding it to a link budget, multiply by the number of turns. A single turn may be a fraction of a dB; several turns can add more than 1 dB, which can exceed the margin of a short link.

items: Find the tightest bend radius R in the route.
Read α_bend per turn at the operating wavelength from the fiber data or a measured curve.
Count the turns N at that radius.
Add N α_bend dB to the loss budget.
If the margin is small, increase R, shorten the route or use bend-insensitive fiber.

blocks.text: Compare this with Chapter 2.1: fiber attenuation is about 0.2 dB/km at 1550 nm, so 1 dB of bend loss equals the attenuation of roughly 5 km of fiber. That is why installation rules matter as much as the fiber's dB/km figure. See Unit 5, Link Design and Fiber Measurements, for the full power budget.

figure.caption: Bend loss per turn falls sharply as the bend radius grows. At 5 mm the curve gives 0.40 dB per turn; at 10 mm it gives 0.020 dB per turn.

spec.aria: A curve of bend loss per turn against bend radius, falling sharply as the radius grows, so small bends are far more costly.

examples.question: A 1550 nm fiber has a measured bend-loss curve α = 8 e^(−0.6R) dB per turn, with R in mm. (a) Find the loss for one turn at R = 5 mm and at R = 10 mm. (b) Find the extra loss when a cable tray forces four turns at R = 5 mm. (c) Say why the same tray hurts less at 1310 nm.
steps: Given: α(R) = 8 e^(−0.6R) dB per turn, with R in mm.
Four turns at R = 5 mm: total extra loss = 4 × 0.3983 = 1.5932 dB ≈ 1.6 dB.
At 1310 nm the same tray hurts less because bending loss rises with wavelength; the shorter 1310 nm wavelength sees lower loss than 1550 nm at the same radius.
examples.answer: One turn loses 0.40 dB at 5 mm and 0.020 dB at 10 mm; four turns at 5 mm add 1.6 dB, and the same tray is less lossy at 1310 nm because bend loss rises with wavelength.
examples.check:
import math

def bend_loss_per_turn(R):
    return 8 * math.exp(-0.6 * R)

l5 = bend_loss_per_turn(5)
l10 = bend_loss_per_turn(10)
l4 = 4 * l5

print(f"{l5:.2f}")
print(f"{l10:.3f}")
print(f"{l4:.1f}")

traps: Bend loss is not worse at shorter wavelength: it rises with wavelength, so 1550 nm suffers more than 1310 nm at the same radius.
α is per turn, not total: multiply by the number of turns before adding it to the link budget.
Macro bending is one large curve; micro bending is many small random curves. Do not treat a tight mandrel test as a micro-bending measurement.
Keep R and B in matching units; if B is per mm, R must be in mm.
Do not add a bend loss in dB to an attenuation coefficient in dB/km as if both were per km.

quiz.q: Define macro bending and micro bending.
quiz.a: Macro bending is loss from one large curve of radius R. Micro bending is loss from many small random bends along the fiber.

quiz.q: Why does a guided mode lose power on the outside of a bend?
quiz.a: The mode field extends into the cladding. On the outside of the curve its phase front tilts and the tail is not held by total internal reflection, so it tunnels out and radiates.

quiz.q: A fiber has α = 8e^(−0.6R) dB per turn, R in mm. Find the loss for two turns at R = 6 mm.
Using the same curve, find the loss for five turns at R = 10 mm.
Why does a 1550 nm link suffer more bend loss than a 1310 nm link at the same radius?
quiz.a: The mode field is wider at longer wavelength, so more field reaches the cladding on the outside of the bend. The loss curve is therefore higher at 1550 nm.

quiz.q: How does a low-index trench in the cladding reduce bend loss?
quiz.a: The trench lowers the cladding index near the core and pulls the mode inward. Less field reaches the outer cladding at a bend, so less power radiates.

quiz.q: Why must a bend-loss figure be multiplied by the number of turns before it enters a link budget?
quiz.a: The quoted α is dB per turn. The total added loss is Nα, and the budget needs the total dB.

beyond: Not for the exam. Bend-insensitive fiber is now common in FTTH and data-center cabling; the G.657 family is the usual search term. Manufacturers quote minimum bend radius at 1550 nm and 1625 nm, because longer wavelengths are more sensitive. The mandrel wrap test is standardized in field practice. Search "macrobending vs microbending", "G.657 fiber" and "mandrel wrap test" for the industrial details.
